Name: subliminal_capacity
Title: How Many Traits Can a Hidden Channel Carry? Measuring the Capacity and Interference of Subliminal Learning
Short Hypothesis: Subliminal learning has a bounded, measurable channel capacity: a single teacher-generated dataset can only transmit a limited number of simultaneously-encoded behavioral traits before the traits interfere destructively and transfer collapses, and this capacity scales with steering-vector orthogonality, dataset size, and layer count rather than with human-semantic distinctness of the traits.
Related Work: Cloud et al. (2025/Nature 2026) introduced subliminal learning for single traits (owl preference, misalignment) via number sequences. Morgulis & Hewitt (2026) show steering-vector teachers transmit complex multi-word biases and that the steering vector itself is transferred, localized to specific layers. Nief et al. (2026) show it is a fragile LoRA/context artifact with an inverted-U rank dependence. Gisler et al. (2026) show transmission survives paraphrase. Madl (2026) shows channel location constrains auditability. All prior work studies transmission of a SINGLE trait at a time (or a single steering direction). No one has asked how many independent traits can be co-transmitted through one subliminal dataset, whether they interfere, and what governs the ceiling. We frame subliminal learning as an information channel and empirically characterize its multi-trait capacity, interference structure, and scaling laws—an entirely new axis distinct from mechanism-explanation, single-trait scope, and auditability papers.
Abstract: Subliminal learning lets a teacher language model covertly pass a behavioral trait—like a preference for owls or misalignment—to a student through semantically unrelated data such as number sequences. Every study so far transmits one trait at a time. We ask a new, elegant question: treating subliminal transmission as a communication channel, how many independent traits can a single teacher-generated dataset carry simultaneously, and what determines that capacity? We build multi-trait teachers by combining multiple steering vectors (e.g., 'love owls' + 'prefer blue' + 'terse' + ... up to 10 traits) and have them generate one shared number/code dataset. We then fine-tune students and measure, per trait, how much of each bias is inherited. We test three hypotheses: (H1) transfer degrades gracefully then collapses as trait count rises, defining a capacity ceiling; (H2) capacity is governed by the pairwise cosine similarity of the underlying steering vectors—near-orthogonal traits coexist, near-parallel traits interfere destructively—rather than by human-semantic similarity; (H3) capacity scales with dataset size, number of steered layers, and LoRA rank in a predictable way, and packing traits into disjoint layers raises the ceiling. We evaluate across Qwen, Llama, and Gemma with LLM-judge trait scoring, and recover per-trait steering vectors from the student to measure interference geometrically. Results yield the first capacity/scaling characterization of the subliminal channel, informing both attackers' packing limits and defenders' expectations of how many hidden behaviors a distillation pipeline could smuggle.
Experiments: 1) Build a bank of 12+ trait steering vectors per base model (Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B) using activation steering trained to maximize likelihood of target-behavior samples (following Morgulis & Hewitt): animal preferences, color, verbosity, formality, a misalignment direction, sycophancy, and multi-word biases. Record pairwise cosine similarities among the vectors. 2) Multi-trait teacher generation: for trait-set sizes k in {1,2,3,5,7,10}, additively combine the corresponding steering vectors (with normalization) into one teacher and generate a shared number-sequence dataset (and a parallel code/math-trace dataset). Include random-subset draws per k and multiple seeds. 3) Student fine-tuning: LoRA and full fine-tuning, Adam and SGD; matched base models plus mismatched-base negative controls. 4) Per-trait measurement: for each trait in the set, score the student's exhibited bias via LLM-judge probability and target-token frequency; compute a normalized transfer rate relative to single-trait baseline. Plot transfer vs k to locate the capacity ceiling (H1). 5) Interference geometry (H2): correlate per-pair transfer degradation with steering-vector cosine similarity and, separately, with human-semantic similarity (embedding distance / judge-rated relatedness); test whether cosine (not semantics) predicts interference. Recover per-trait steering vectors from the student dataset and measure cosine to originals to quantify degradation. 6) Scaling knobs (H3): sweep dataset size (1k/5k/20k/100k examples), number of steered layers (few vs many, overlapping vs disjoint layer assignments), and LoRA rank (4-64); fit simple scaling curves for capacity. Test the 'disjoint-layer packing' intervention: assign each trait to a distinct layer band and measure whether the ceiling rises. 7) Baselines/controls: prompt-based (system-prompt) multi-trait teacher vs steering-vector teacher; clean (no-steering) control. Metrics: per-trait normalized transfer rate, aggregate 'traits successfully transmitted' count at threshold, transfer-vs-k curves, correlation coefficients (transfer degradation vs vector cosine and vs semantic similarity), recovered-vector cosine alignment, and benign-task retention (GSM8K/HumanEval subsets).
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Combining steering vectors additively may distort each trait even before distillation, confounding capacity with steering artifacts; mitigated by measuring the teacher's own multi-trait behavior as an upper bound and normalizing student transfer to it. 2) Nief et al. show subliminal transfer is fragile w.r.t. LoRA rank and context, so multi-trait transfer could be weak/noisy; we use the strongest known regimes (steering-vector teachers, matched contexts) and multiple seeds. 3) Layer-disjoint packing may not be cleanly separable in practice, weakening H3's intervention. 4) LLM-judge scoring of many co-present traits may be noisy, especially when traits conflict (e.g., terse vs verbose); we pre-screen for compatible trait sets and report judge agreement. 5) Results may be model-family or scale specific; three base models mitigate but do not guarantee frontier generality.
